GBR.story:
In 1958 someone first reported the BBC broadcaster Jimmy Savile to police. Surrey Police investigated him in 2007–09 and brought no charges, and in December 2011, two months after his death, the BBC shelved a Newsnight investigation into him. Only after an ITV documentary in October 2012 did the Metropolitan Police open an investigation. Its January 2013 report with the NSPCC recorded 214 crimes across 28 police force areas from 1955 to 2009; 450 people had made allegations, 73% of them under 18 at the time. It found no clear evidence that he was part of a paedophile ring.

In 1968 a pupil told police about Cyril Smith, later Liberal MP for Rochdale, and was told Smith was “a very important, powerful man”. The prosecutors advised against charges in 1970, and reviews in 1998 and 1999 led nowhere. Smith was knighted in 1988 though Margaret Thatcher had been told of the allegations. He died in 2010, never charged; in 2012 prosecutors said he should have been. In the same town in 2008, a girl went to police about men linked to two takeaways, and prosecutors declined to act, questioning her credibility. Nine men were convicted in 2012, and a 2024 review found children had been “left at the mercy” of gangs from 2004 to 2013.

Institutions often dealt with abusers by moving them. In 1982 an internal report for the Iwerne Trust, which ran evangelical camps, described the beatings John Smyth QC gave boys. Police were not told until 2013. Smyth moved to Zimbabwe in 1984 and ran camps for boys there. The 2024 Makin review found an “active cover-up” and called him “a problem solved and exported to Africa”; Archbishop Justin Welby resigned five days after it was published. Fettes College in Edinburgh dismissed the teacher Iain Wares in 1979 with a glowing reference, and he went on to abuse children in South Africa.

The state itself sent about 4,000 children from British care to Australian institutions between 1945 and 1970, where the national inquiry (IICSA) found extensive evidence of abuse. Some claims did not hold up: an inquiry found no evidence that MI5 used Belfast's Kincora home for blackmail, and Carl Beech, who invented a Westminster “VIP ring”, was himself jailed. Today IJM UK names Britain among the top three consumers of livestreamed abuse of Filipino children. England and Wales removed the three-year legal deadline for abuse claims only in June 2026.

For a novice, the British record shows that reports were usually made, sometimes decades early. What failed was what police, prosecutors, churches and broadcasters did with them, and the status of the accused often decided that. In any new case, ask when the first complaint was made and who received it.

IND.story:
In April 2018 researchers from the Tata Institute of Social Sciences handed the Bihar government an audit of 110 children's homes in 38 districts. They graded a girls' home in Muzaffarpur, run by a state-funded charity under Brajesh Thakur, as “criminal negligence”, and raised abuse at 14 other homes. At one audited home, staff told the team the key to the complaint box had been lost. A police complaint (an FIR, the first report that starts a criminal case) followed on 31 May 2018. Medical checks indicated sexual abuse of 34 girls, most of them children. The district child protection officer was among the accused, and the state's welfare minister, Manju Verma, resigned. Because the accused were influential in Bihar, the Supreme Court moved the trial to Delhi, where Thakur and 18 others were convicted in January 2020. The federal police (CBI) later cleared Verma, a finding the magazine The Caravan disputes.

The same summer, in Deoria, Uttar Pradesh, a 10-year-old girl escaped to a women's police station and said girls were taken away in cars in the afternoon and brought back crying in the morning. Police rescued 24 girls. The state had cut the charity's funding a year earlier, yet the home kept running. In Unnao, a girl accused Kuldeep Singh Sengar, a BJP state legislator, of rape in 2017. Her father died in police custody, and Sengar was arrested only after the High Court ordered it. He was convicted in 2019; his sentence was suspended in 2025, and in May 2026 the Supreme Court set that suspension aside.

India also sent 12,511 children abroad for adoption from 2003 to 2022. In 2001 Hyderabad police stopped a man carrying three baby girls for a home that had earned Rs 3.33 crore from foreign adoptions; ten people were convicted in 2005. In Chennai a family-run agency was suspected of trafficking more than 350 children. Australia froze adoptions through some Indian agencies in 2008. Girls also arrive from Nepal across an open 1,850 km border, an estimated 5,000–10,000 a year, and from Bangladesh. When a Minnesota diocese sent the priest Joseph Jeyapaul back to India in 2005, his Indian bishop kept him in ministry; he was extradited in 2014.

India has held no national inquiry into institutional abuse, and South Asia has no representative survey of online abuse. What the record holds came from one university audit, one escaped child, and court orders. When cases surface only this way, ask who audits the homes the state funds, and what happens to the complaint box.

ESP.story:
After Spain's Civil War ended in 1939, about 30,000 children were placed in state care under the Franco regime. In the words of a 2008 ruling by Judge Baltasar Garzón, most were “war orphans with parents who were dead, imprisoned, exiled, in hiding, or disappeared”. Their names were changed so they could be given to families loyal to the regime. Unmarried mothers held in homes run by the Women's Protection Board were pressured to give up their babies. A 1977 amnesty law has hindered investigation, and many of that board's files went missing in 1996.

In 2011 families of 261 babies who disappeared from hospitals asked the attorney general to investigate a network of doctors and nurses, and lawyers claimed up to 300,000 babies were taken. The first trial came in 2018. A Madrid court found the gynaecologist Eduardo Vela responsible for taking a newborn and forging her birth certificate in 1969, then acquitted him because the statute of limitations, the legal deadline to prosecute, had run out. In 2026 forensic geneticists at a national institute found no evidence of systematic theft from hospitals and called the 300,000 figure a hoax. They did not deny the coercion inside Francoist institutions or the 30,000 children in state care.

Spain's first official inquiry into abuse in the Catholic Church was carried out by the Ombudsman, who presented a nearly 800-page report to parliament on 27 October 2023 after collecting 487 testimonies. A survey of 8,013 adults found 11.7% had been abused before 18, 1.13% in religious settings and 0.6% by a priest or religious. The Ombudsman did not turn these into a total; media did, putting it at about 440,000. The bishops apologised and disputed the media figures.

Spain also appears as the home country of an offender. In 2011 Morocco sentenced the retired Spanish professor Daniel Galván to 30 years for raping 11 children aged 4 to 14. In 2013 King Mohammed VI pardoned him among 48 Spanish prisoners, and Galván left on an expired passport. The pardon was revoked after protests, and he was arrested in Spain. Spain is also a destination for Nigerian and Romanian girls trafficked into prostitution, and received 39 Romanian children for adoption in 2002.

For a novice, Spain shows two kinds of numbers side by side: a figure that grew past the evidence, and survey figures that were never turned into a count of victims. When a case fails because a deadline passed, ask who set the deadline and when the child could first have spoken.

COD.story:
In March and May 2004, Congolese women and the media reported that UN peacekeepers in Bunia, in eastern DR Congo, were having sex with local girls. UN investigators (OIOS) spent May to September there. They found sexual contact with peacekeepers happened “with regularity”, usually for food or small sums of money, and that many cases involved girls under 18, some as young as 13. Of 72 allegations, many were too vague to investigate and six were fully proven. Under UN rules, soldiers are tried by their own country, and the UN's 2025 data show few such cases finished; one Togolese officer was sent home and jailed for 60 days.

Fifteen years later the pattern returned with aid. During the 2018–2020 Ebola response in North Kivu and Ituri, an independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators, 21 of them established with certainty as WHO employees. Most were temporary local hires who offered jobs in exchange for sex. The youngest person heard was a 13-year-old girl selling phone cards in Mangina, who said a WHO driver raped her. Twenty-nine women and girls became pregnant. Congo's own army has also been accused abroad: in 2015 Congolese troops serving in the Central African Republic faced 17 allegations involving 15 child victims, and the battalion was withdrawn in January 2016.

The war has taken children directly. In 2012 the International Criminal Court's first ever conviction was of Thomas Lubanga, for using children under 15 as soldiers in Ituri; sexual violence against girl soldiers was raised at trial but never charged. In 2019 Bosco Ntaganda became the first person the court convicted of sexual slavery. In December 2009 the Lord's Resistance Army killed at least 321 people around Makombo and abducted 250, at least 80 of them children. In 2024 alone the UN verified sexual violence against 358 girls, by M23, CODECO, the national army and other groups, and the abduction of 815 children. Children also work and are sexually exploited at eastern mines, with government officials among those named.

DR Congo sent 3,483 children abroad for adoption from 2003 to 2022 and suspended exit permits in 2013. Its region has no survey of online abuse at all.

For a novice, Congo shows that the people sent to protect or feed children can become a risk, and that punishment depends on another country's courts. When a mission reports allegations, ask how many cases were finished and by whom.

NGA.story:
On the night of 14 April 2014, Boko Haram gunmen entered the dormitories of the girls' secondary school in Chibok, Borno state, and loaded 276 girls onto trucks. More than 50 jumped from the lorries and escaped within hours. Ten years later, Amnesty International said 82 were still captive and that 20 released girls had been forced to marry former fighters. The raids continued. In February 2018 militants took 110 schoolgirls from Dapchi; the government said 106 children were freed a month later and denied paying a ransom. In December 2020 gunmen took over 300 boys from a school in Kankara. In 2024 alone the UN verified the abduction of 991 children in Nigeria and sexual violence, all of it forced marriage, against 419.

A second trade runs through clinics posing as orphanages, which Nigerian police call “baby farms”. In 2011 police in Aba freed 32 pregnant girls, mostly aged 15–17, allegedly held so their babies could be sold; four babies already sold were recovered. In 2018 Lagos officials said 162 children had been rescued from a “baby factory” and two unregistered orphanages. Nigeria sent 3,263 children abroad for adoption from 2003 to 2022, and adoption from Nigeria remains open.

Girls also leave the country. The 2025 US trafficking report says organised groups, some tied to Nigerian cult organisations, move women and girls into prostitution in Italy, Spain and the UK, and to gold-mining areas of Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire. Most are from Edo State and go overland through Niger and Libya, held by debts and oaths; the UN's migration agency recorded an almost 600 per cent rise in likely victims arriving in Italy by sea from 2014 to 2017. The same report names corruption among anti-trafficking officials as a significant concern.

The direction can reverse online. Two brothers in Lagos posed as a girl on hacked Instagram accounts, got explicit images from a 17-year-old in Michigan and demanded $1,000; he died by suicide in March 2022. They were extradited and each sentenced to 17.5 years. West and Central Africa has no survey data on online abuse.

For a novice, Nigeria's cases mostly surface after a raid or a rescue, which counts the children found, not the ones still held. Ask how many children were taken and how many were ever brought back.

ITA.story:
In 2009 a priest named Nicola Corradi was accused of abuse at the Provolo school for deaf children in Verona. The diocese flagged him in 2011. By then he was working at the same religious order's school in Mendoza, Argentina. Police there arrested him in 2016, and in 2019 an Argentine court sentenced him to 42 years for abusing deaf children. Italy also worked the other way, as a hiding place. Joseph Henn, a priest indicted in Arizona in 2003, went to Italy and avoided an approved extradition until his arrest in Rome in May 2019.

Italy has never held a national inquiry into abuse in church or state institutions, and “there are no official statistics”. In May 2012 the Italian Bishops' Conference said that under the Lateran concordat, the treaty between Italy and the Vatican, its priests have no obligation to report suspected abuse to the police. The victims' group Rete l'Abuso has asked for years for an independent inquiry from outside the church. Italy has one of the largest Catholic populations in the world, yet the record of what happened inside its parishes and schools comes mostly from other countries' courts.

Italy appears on the map in other roles. It received children through adoption systems later found to be corrupt: 383 from South Korea between 1965 and 2008, where a 2025 truth commission found state-enabled fraud, and 39 from Romania in 2002, two years before Romania banned foreign adoption. Some children taken by El Salvador's armed forces during its civil war were adopted to Italy. It is the main destination for women and girls from Edo State in Nigeria, moved through Niger and Libya and across the sea, held by debts and oaths. And a 2006 study in Kenya found Italian, German and Swiss tourists made up 44 per cent of the clients of children exploited on the Kenyan coast.

For a novice, an empty record for Italy does not mean nothing happened. It means no one official was asked to count, and church rules said priests did not have to tell police. When a country has no inquiry, ask who would have to order one and who benefits from waiting.

CHE.story:
In 1926 the Swiss foundation Pro Juventute began a programme it called the Charity for the Children of the Country Road. Until 1973 it took about 600 Yenish children, from a travelling community, away from their families and placed them in homes and foster families. Around 2,000 Traveller children are believed to have been affected by such measures in all. The foundation did not act alone: officials at every level of government shared staff with it and helped fund it. On 20 February 2025 the Swiss government accepted a legal opinion that this persecution was a crime against humanity under current international law, and repeated its apology.

The Yenish children were one part of a larger system. From about 1930 to 1981, Swiss cantons and towns placed more than 60,000 people in about 650 institutions without any court order. Some children were sent to farms as indentured labourers, known as Verdingkinder. An independent expert commission reported in September 2019 that people held this way were abused physically, psychologically and sexually. The government had apologised in 2010, and a 2016 law gave each victim a payment of CHF 25,000.

Switzerland also brought children in. It received 1,111 South Korean children between 1968 and 1997. From the 1970s to 2000, Swiss authorities approved adoptions from Sri Lanka, India and Tibet, often of children wrongly described as orphans, on incomplete or forged papers; in Sri Lanka in the 1980s, babies were bought or taken from hospitals and paid “acting mothers” posed as their birth mothers in court. The Federal Council admitted the authorities' failings in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 recommended banning intercountry adoption entirely.

Swiss men also appear as travelling offenders. Repeat offenders from Switzerland, already convicted at home, abused boys in Pattaya, Thailand.

For a novice, the Swiss cases show that much harm to children was ordered by officials, written down, and lawful at the time. Ask who signed the placement or the adoption papers, and whether anyone checked them.

ZAF.story:
In 1979 Fettes College in Edinburgh dismissed a teacher named Iain Wares and gave him a glowing reference. He moved to South Africa, taught there, and later abused children. South Africa approved his extradition to Scotland, which he was still fighting in 2025. A German priest, Georg Kerkhoff, came the same way: with abuse cases pending at home, he worked for years in South Africa and was tried for abusing boys at a 2008 camp before being sent back and jailed in Krefeld in 2015.

The longest-running case arrived from Zimbabwe. John Smyth QC had beaten boys at English evangelical camps; a church report described it in 1982, and he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984 and ran camps for boys there. Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, he moved to South Africa in 2001 and attended churches in Durban and then Cape Town, at Church on Main from 2004 to 2016. The 2024 Makin review found it highly likely he kept abusing until his death in Cape Town on 11 August 2018. He was never charged anywhere.

Other cases begin inside the country. The pastor Timothy Omotoso was first reported in 2017 and acted on the same year, but mistrial motions and judges stepping aside delayed his trial for eight years. A whistleblower in the case, Pamela Mabini, was shot dead on 7 March 2025, weeks before the verdict. The 2025 US trafficking report says traffickers recruit children from rural areas into brothels in Gauteng and Western Cape and use drugs to control them, and that some parents sell their children for sex or online abuse. Migrants moved along a “Southern Route” from a refugee camp in Malawi also end up in South Africa's sex trade. South Africa sent 3,716 children abroad for adoption from 2003 to 2022.

For a novice, South Africa shows what happens when one country deals with an abuser by letting him leave: another country inherits him, without warning. Ask whether a school or church that dismisses someone tells the next employer, and the police, why.

BGR.story:
In 2007 a BBC film by Kate Blewett, “Bulgaria's Abandoned Children”, showed disabled children neglected at the state home in Mogilino. In February 2008 Bulgaria's social affairs minister repeated a promise to close it and six similar homes, and by June children were being moved out. No sexual-abuse finding about Mogilino was found; it is a record of neglect. But Bulgaria has had one of the highest numbers of children in state institutions in the EU, and the 2025 US trafficking report cites a UN special rapporteur who found sexual exploitation, including possible trafficking, common among children in those homes. The same report says Bulgarian women and girls are sold for sex across Western Europe, in Sofia and in resort and border towns. Courts convicted 31 traffickers; only eight went to prison, and 34 convicted traffickers received suspended sentences. It calls corruption in police and courts pervasive.

Bulgaria's police also appear on the other side. In Operation Blackwrist, which began in 2017, Bulgaria's cybercrime unit took down the servers of a subscription website that published the abuse of boys in Thailand every week to nearly 63,000 users. Its administrators in Thailand and Australia were sentenced to 146 years and to 40 years and three months.

In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British group that finds and removes abuse material, took action against 87,959 web addresses hosted in Bulgaria. That was 28% of everything it acted on worldwide, up from 9% the year before, and it said the rise came from “just a few particular sites”. The servers are in Bulgaria; the people uploading and paying may be anywhere.

Bulgaria sent 5,067 children abroad for adoption from 2003 to 2022, and 2,649 children adopted from Sofia received US visas from 1994 to 2014. Adoption remains open.

For a novice, Bulgaria shows two separate things: children left in large state homes, and a country's servers used by a handful of sites. Neither shows up as a local abuse case, so ask who inspects the homes and who rents out the servers.

NPL.story:
In the Karnali region of rural Nepal, agents take money from families with a promise to put their children in school, then deliver the children to children's homes in Kathmandu, which pay the agents a commission. Charities documented one child admitted with a forged certificate saying a parent had died. UNICEF estimates about 85% of children in Nepal's registered homes have a living parent or guardian.

Those homes fed foreign adoption. In March 2007 a Daily Telegraph investigation described babies being bought, bribes paid and birth families deceived. A month later Nepal's new minister stopped all intercountry adoptions, leaving about 400 Western families waiting. New rules came in 2008, and the US later suspended adoptions of children declared abandoned because the papers could not be trusted. Nepal sent 1,991 children abroad from 2003 to 2022.

The largest movement of children runs south, across a 1,850 km border with India that is open with no checks. Researchers estimate 5,000–10,000 Nepali women and girls are trafficked to India each year, to brothels in Kolkata, Mumbai's Kamathipura district and elsewhere, recruited with false offers of jobs, marriage or online romance. The 2025 US trafficking report says Nepali courts convicted 406 traffickers in a year, and cites a 2024 study finding most workers in Nepal's adult entertainment sector were trafficking victims, nearly half of them children. It also reports traffickers bribing some Indian officials to fly Nepali workers to other countries. Foreign aid workers have also offended inside Nepal: a Canadian working with street children abused boys at his home there.

South Asia has no representative survey of online child abuse, so the scale of abuse through phones and the internet in Nepal is not known.

For a novice, Nepal shows how a promise of schooling or a job is the usual first step. When a children's home is full of children with living parents, ask who brought them there and who was paid.

BIH.story:
In 1992, in the Serb-held town of Foča, Bosniak women and girls were held at sites such as the Partizan Sports Hall, beside the town's police building, and taken from there to flats and houses to be raped. The UN war crimes tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) later found that Bosnian Serb forces used rape as an instrument of terror and that local police guarded the women and joined in. In February 2001 it sentenced Dragoljub Kunarac to 28 years, Radomir Kovač to 20 years, including for holding two girls in his flat for about four months and selling victims to other soldiers, and Zoran Vuković to 12 years, including for raping a girl he knew to be 15.

From 1995, with international police and soldiers in the country to keep the peace, a market for women and girls grew around them. Human Rights Watch reported in 2002 that women and girls, mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine, were sold to Bosnian bar owners and held by debts in bars and brothels. Local police were found acting as owners, guards and customers. Eighteen monitors from the UN police task force who bought women, visited brothels or faced trafficking-related charges were sent home, and none was confirmed prosecuted. A US Army report documented employees of DynCorp, a US contractor, buying women; one admitted buying a woman for 1,600 Deutschmarks. DynCorp fired the UN monitor Kathryn Bolkovac in April 2001 after she reported the trafficking. In August 2002 a British employment tribunal found the dismissal unfair. Sending the men home also meant they could not be used as witnesses.

For a novice, Bosnia shows how immunity works in practice: foreign police and contractors were removed from the country rather than put on trial there. When peacekeepers or contractors are accused, ask which court has power over them and whether it ever sat.

MAR.story:
In December 2010 Moroccan police arrested Daniel Galván, a retired Spanish professor. In September 2011 a court sentenced him to 30 years for raping 11 Moroccan children aged 4 to 14. On 30 July 2013 King Mohammed VI pardoned 48 Spanish prisoners as a gesture to Spain, and Galván was among them. He left Morocco on an expired passport, with the authorities' knowledge. Protesters gathered outside parliament in Rabat and were violently dispersed. On 4 August the king revoked the pardon, citing the seriousness of the crimes and the victims' rights, and said he had not been told the details of the case. By then Galván was in Spain, where he was arrested and imprisoned to finish his sentence.

It had happened before. A 2010 US diplomatic cable reported that in 2006 the king pardoned Hervé Le Gloannec, a Frenchman convicted of abusing a 15-year-old boy in Marrakesh, and he was released.

Foreign offenders still come. The 2025 US trafficking report says charities find tourists exploiting children in Tangier in holiday rentals owned and managed by Europeans. Morocco also sends soldiers abroad: Moroccan military personnel are named in UN tables of sexual exploitation and abuse allegations in the peacekeeping missions in the Central African Republic and DR Congo, where soldiers are tried only by their own country.

The Middle East and North Africa has no representative survey of online child abuse, so how often children in Morocco are abused through the internet is not measured.

For a novice, the Galván case shows that a conviction can be undone by a political decision made for reasons unrelated to the children involved. When a pardon or a transfer is announced as diplomacy, ask who was on the list and who checked it.

SRB.story:
Over four years, the group Mental Disability Rights International visited Serbia's state institutions for people with mental disabilities, which held more than 17,000 people. Its report, “Torment not Treatment”, released on 14 November 2007, described children and adults tied to beds or kept in cribs for years, filthy rooms, infectious disease and no outside oversight, treatment it called “tantamount to torture”. It warned of sexual exploitation: at Vršac, men and women lived in mixed wards, and staff said they made no effort to find out whether sex was consensual. In 2006 the director of one institution refused to open a locked area and asked the investigators to leave. Serbian officials called the findings “dark propaganda”.

Serbia was also a route. After NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in Kosovo in 1999, Amnesty International reported in 2004 that women and girls were trafficked into forced prostitution there, brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia through Serbia. Amnesty said the international presence produced 80% of the traffickers' income at the time, and found no criminal case against any soldier in his home country.

The map also lists Serbia among the places connected to Nazi Germany's programme of seizing children judged “racially valuable” and giving them new identities in German families. In 1948 a US military tribunal at Nuremberg convicted 13 SS officials for it.

Serbia has no case on this map in which a court or inquiry found sexual abuse of children inside its own institutions. The 2007 report is an outside investigation, and the risk it described was never followed by a public count.

For a novice, Serbia shows how places that hold children with disabilities stay closed: a locked door, no inspections, and officials who deny the report. Ask who has the right to walk into an institution unannounced, and whether anyone has done it since.

BDI.story:
In 2016 UN investigators went to Dékoa, a town in the Central African Republic, to look into two allegations against peacekeepers from Burundi and Gabon serving in the UN mission there. They interviewed some 136 alleged victims, 48% of all victims the UN recorded that year. Press accounts said at least 98 girls described abuse and 41 soldiers were identified and sent home without charges. The UN's own tables list allegations against Burundian troops involving 46 children. Under UN rules, peacekeepers can be tried only by their own country, and the Secretary-General's 2017 report said Burundi's and Gabon's investigations were still pending.

Burundian soldiers were also named earlier in Somalia. In September 2014 Human Rights Watch, after 50 interviews, documented rapes and sexual exploitation by African Union soldiers in Mogadishu, mostly by Ugandan troops at the mission's headquarters and Burundian troops at their own base. Four of the rapes and one sexual assault were of girls under 18. Many of the women and girls had come to the bases for medicine or aid, and some were pushed into sex in exchange for money, food or medicine. Interpreters helped the soldiers reach them.

At home, almost nothing reaches the international reporting systems. In 2025 the US clearinghouse for online child abuse reports (NCMEC) received 1,028 reports linked to Burundi. That is a count of what tech companies flagged, not a measure of abuse inside the country.

For a novice, Burundi shows how the countries that send soldiers also decide whether those soldiers face trial. When a contingent is sent home, ask whether a court in the home country ever opened a case.

AUT.story:
From 1948 to 1977 the City of Vienna ran a children's home at Wilhelminenberg; from 1962 it held only girls. In June 2013 a commission set up by the city presented a 344-page report built on 217 interviews, 140 of them with former residents. It found the girls were widely abused, including rape and sexual exploitation by caregivers and by men from outside, with victims as young as about six. Staff in the city department that oversaw the home knew of the abuse and did not act, and city politicians who learned of it in the 1960s ignored it. The findings went to prosecutors, and some former residents were paid up to €35,000.

The church reckoning began three years earlier. In spring 2010 Austria's bishops set up an independent commission for victims, known as the Klasnic Commission after its chair. It set four levels of compensation: €5,000, €15,000, €25,000, and more in extreme cases. A commission chosen by the institution that faces the claims is not the same as an inquiry with the power to compel evidence.

Austria is also a destination. The 2025 US trafficking report names Austria among the countries where Romanian women and girls are exploited, and says girls in Romania's state homes, especially homes for people with disabilities, are at risk.

For a novice, the Vienna report shows that the people responsible for overseeing a home can know about abuse for years and do nothing, and that it took the city's own commission, decades later, to say so. When a payment scheme is announced, ask who set the amounts and who decided which cases count.

MLI.story:
Mali has been at war with armed groups for years, and the UN keeps a yearly count of attacks on children there. In 2024 it verified the rape of 32 girls. It could not identify who did it in 22 cases; four were by the Islamic State in the Greater Sahara, three by the al-Qaeda-linked group JNIM, two by Mali's own army and one by the militia Ganda Lassal Izo. It also verified the abduction of 119 children, four of them by foreign security personnel working in the country. In 2023 it had verified the rape of 15 girls, four by Mali's army.

These are verified cases, meaning the UN confirmed each one itself. In a conflict zone, many cases never reach anyone who can confirm them, so the true numbers are higher by an unknown amount.

Mali is also a destination. The 2025 US trafficking report says organised Nigerian networks, some tied to cult groups, move Nigerian women and girls to gold-mining areas in Mali, Senegal, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire for prostitution. West and Central Africa has no representative survey of online child abuse.

For a novice, Mali's record shows that the soldiers meant to protect children appear in the same list as the groups they are fighting. When you see a yearly UN figure, remember it counts only what investigators could reach and confirm.

MDG.story:
When Mozambique tightened its laws against child sex tourism, observers recorded the trade growing in Madagascar instead, with mostly French and Italian offenders. The 2025 US trafficking report says most children sold for sex in Madagascar are exploited by Malagasy men, but foreign tourists, often from France, also abuse children there. Some parents encourage their daughters into paid sex with tourists, and children are exploited in karaoke bars in the capital, Antananarivo.

The island of Nosy Be, a tourist destination, has its own anti-trafficking committee. In July 2025 police there arrested two women suspected of filming the abuse of their own children and selling the videos to foreign buyers, paid by mobile phone money transfer; they were charged. In the year the US report covers, Madagascar's courts convicted 15 traffickers, the first convictions in four years. The report calls corruption and officials' involvement significant concerns, and says one official was investigated.

For a novice, Madagascar shows how enforcement in one country can push offenders to the next one with weaker policing, and how the same trade can move from hotels to phones. When one country's numbers fall, ask where the offenders went.

HUN.story:
In 2022 a Hungarian court sentenced Endre Kónya, the former deputy director of the children's home in Bicske, to three years and four months. He had helped the home's director cover up the director's sexual abuse of children. In April 2023, before a visit by the Pope, President Katalin Novák pardoned about two dozen people, and Kónya was one of them. The justice minister, Judit Varga, countersigned the pardon. No one announced it.

The news site Telex reported the pardon on 2 February 2024. Protests followed. On 10 February Novák resigned, saying she had made a mistake, and Varga announced the same day that she was leaving public life. Prime Minister Viktor Orbán proposed changing the constitution so that no one convicted of crimes against children could be pardoned.

Hungary also sends children abroad for adoption: 2,868 from 2003 to 2022, and the system remains open.

For a novice, the Bicske case shows that a conviction for hiding abuse can be erased quietly, by the highest office in the country, and that in this case it came to light only because a journalist found it nearly a year later. Ask whether pardons in your country are published, and who checks what crime each one covers.

PSE.story:
In June 2024 the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Israel, a body set up by the UN Human Rights Council, reported its findings on sexual violence in the war that began in October 2023. It found that Israeli security forces subjected Palestinians to sexual and gender-based violence, including forced public nudity and sexualised torture, during arrests and in detention, and that “men and boys were targeted in particular ways”. It found the persecution of Palestinian men and boys on the basis of gender to be a crime against humanity.

The same commission found that sexual violence was committed during the attacks of 7 October 2023 at the Nova festival, at Nahal Oz and at several kibbutzim, and that 252 people, including 36 children, were taken hostage.

This map records the war only to the extent of these UN findings. It has no counts of individual cases of abuse of Palestinian children, and the Middle East and North Africa has no representative survey of online child abuse.

For a novice, the commission's report shows that sexual violence against children in a war is not only a crime against girls; it found boys were targeted too. When you read about abuse in a conflict, ask which body investigated, whether it had access, and what exactly it found.

VIR.story:
Jeffrey Epstein owned Little St. James, a private island in the US Virgin Islands, and lawsuits describe a sex-trafficking operation run partly from it between 1998 and 2019, with girls brought from the US mainland. After his death, the territory's government went after the money around him. It reached a $105m settlement with his estate and a $62.5m settlement with the billionaire Leon Black.

In December 2022 it sued JPMorgan Chase, Epstein's bank, claiming the bank ignored warning signs and helped his activities by keeping him as a client. In June 2023 JPMorgan agreed to pay $290m to nearly 200 of Epstein's victims in a group lawsuit, and in September 2023 to pay the Virgin Islands $75m. Earlier, in July 2020, New York's financial regulator had fined Deutsche Bank $150m for ignoring red flags about Epstein. British regulators permanently banned the former JPMorgan banker Jes Staley for recklessly misleading them about his relationship with Epstein, a ban upheld in June 2025.

All of these are civil settlements and regulatory penalties. None is a criminal finding.

For a novice, the Virgin Islands case shows another way to follow abuse: through the banks that moved the money. When a wealthy person is accused, ask which institutions kept doing business with them, and what warnings they had.

TUR.story:
Türkiye has hosted about 2.9 million Syrians displaced by the war next door. The 2025 US trafficking report says that among them, Syrian girls are married off in unofficial religious ceremonies, particularly in poor rural areas. Because these marriages are not registered with the state, no official record shows a child was married. After the ceremony, the report says, the girls are forced into domestic servitude and sex trafficking. Families and brokers arrange the marriages.

The same report says Türkiye reported no investigations of officials involved in trafficking, though it calls corruption and complicity significant concerns.

Türkiye has also been a destination for a longer time. In March 2007 the US State Department reported that women and children from Moldova were trafficked for sexual exploitation, increasingly to Russia and the Middle East, including Türkiye, Israel and the United Arab Emirates. UNICEF found that children leaving Moldova's residential institutions were several times more likely to be trafficked than other children.

For a novice, the Syrian case shows how a marriage that is never registered can hide the trafficking of a child, because no paperwork ever names her. When refugee numbers are large, ask who is checking the marriages that happen outside the law.

SAU.story:
Saudi Arabia has no case of its own on this map. It appears through the movements of other people. The 2025 US trafficking report says organised begging rings exploit Ethiopian women and children in Saudi Arabia, sending them onto the streets to beg. Saudi Arabia also sits in the region the same report links to tourists who travel out to abuse girls: in Puncak, in West Java, Indonesia, it says Middle Eastern tourists pay for short “contract marriages” with girls as young as nine.

What happens to children inside the country is not counted in the sources this map uses. Childlight, a research centre that pulls together surveys of child sexual abuse, found in its 2026 update that the Middle East and North Africa have no representative surveys of online child sexual exploitation. Its estimates rest on such surveys from only 60 countries.

For a novice, a blank map tile for Saudi Arabia means no one has measured, not that nothing is happening. The cases that are recorded show children moving in and men moving out. Ask what a country would need to publish before its numbers could be compared with anyone else's.

DJI.story:
Djibouti sits on the route out of Ethiopia toward the Red Sea and the Arabian Peninsula. The 2025 US trafficking report says Ethiopian girls are exploited there, and in Sudan, as unpaid domestic workers and in sex trafficking. That is the only recorded case touching Djibouti on this map, and it comes from a report about Ethiopia, not from Djibouti's own records.

The region has no measurement of online abuse. Childlight, a research centre that pulls together surveys of child sexual abuse, found in its 2026 update that the Middle East and North Africa lack representative surveys of online child sexual exploitation. Its estimates rest on such surveys from only 60 countries. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied data for 2023.

For a novice, Djibouti shows how a transit country can stay almost invisible: the girls pass through or are held in homes, and the only trace is a line in another country's report. Ask who counts children who cross a border with no papers.

LVA.story:
On 1 July 2022 a Latvian law took effect that prevents adoptions of Latvian children to the United States, according to the US government's adoption report for 2024. The packet for Latvia holds no case explaining the reason for the law, and none is added here.

The wider pattern is that intercountry adoption moved from one sending country to the next as each was examined. Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2007–08, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia, which banned foreign adoption in 2018, were each closed after inquiries found children bought, stolen or wrongly registered as orphans. Latvia appears on this map as one of the sending countries that later closed a route, without a documented scandal behind it in these sources.

For a novice, a closed adoption route does not always mean wrongdoing was found; sometimes the reason is not recorded. Ask a country that stops adoptions what it found, and whether the children already sent abroad were ever checked on.

RWA.story:
On 10 October 2007 Ireland's Adoption Board suspended adoptions from Ethiopia and Rwanda. That is the only entry for Rwanda on this map, and the packet does not record the reason.

The wider pattern explains why such suspensions happen. Intercountry adoption moved from one sending country to the next as each was examined: Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2007–08, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia, which banned foreign adoption in 2018. Each was closed after inquiries found children bought, stolen or wrongly registered as orphans. Receiving countries decide on their own when to stop accepting children from a place, and they often do so without publishing a finding about each one.

For a novice, Rwanda's single line shows a receiving country pulling back without saying publicly what it saw. Ask what Ireland's board knew in 2007, and whether anyone followed the children already placed.

GNB.story:
Guinea-Bissau has no recorded case on this map. That does not mean nothing happens there. It means the sources this map relies on hold no measurement for it.

Childlight, a research centre that pulls together surveys of child sexual abuse, found in its 2026 update that West and Central Africa have no representative surveys of online child sexual exploitation. Its global estimates rest on such surveys from only 60 countries. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied data for 2023. In 2025, 14% of the 23.4 million reports to the US clearinghouse for online child abuse reports could not be placed in any country at all.

A country can stay blank for several reasons: no survey has been done, police do not report to international systems, or few people use the platforms that send reports.

For a novice, a country with no data is a question, not an answer. Ask whether anyone has ever surveyed children there, and who would pay for it.

KWT.story:
Kuwait has no recorded case on this map. The sources it uses hold no measurement of child sexual abuse or trafficking in the country.

Childlight, a research centre that pulls together surveys of child sexual abuse, found in its 2026 update that the Middle East and North Africa have no representative surveys of online child sexual exploitation. Its global estimates rest on such surveys from only 60 countries. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied data for 2023. In 2025, 14% of the 23.4 million reports to the US clearinghouse for online child abuse reports could not be placed in any country.

Without a survey, the only numbers are cases that police choose to report or journalists uncover, and none of those for Kuwait reached this map.

For a novice, a blank country means no one has measured, not that children there are safe. Ask whether the government has ever run a survey of children, and whether it shares its police data with international systems.

IRN.story:
Iran has no recorded case on this map. The sources it uses hold no measurement of child sexual abuse or trafficking in the country.

Childlight, a research centre that pulls together surveys of child sexual abuse, found in its 2026 update that the Middle East and North Africa have no representative surveys of online child sexual exploitation. Its global estimates rest on such surveys from only 60 countries. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied data for 2023. In 2025, 14% of the 23.4 million reports to the US clearinghouse for online child abuse reports could not be placed in any country.

When a country does not take part in these surveys and reporting systems, its children drop out of the global totals, and the totals look smaller than they are.

For a novice, a blank country is a gap in the record, not a clean record. Ask who has been allowed to survey children there, and who would publish the results.

TGO.story:
Togo has no recorded case on this map. The sources it uses hold no measurement of child sexual abuse or trafficking inside the country.

Childlight, a research centre that pulls together surveys of child sexual abuse, found in its 2026 update that West and Central Africa have no representative surveys of online child sexual exploitation. Its global estimates rest on such surveys from only 60 countries. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied data for 2023. In 2025, 14% of the 23.4 million reports to the US clearinghouse for online child abuse reports could not be placed in any country.

The map's record is thickest where people looked, and in this region few have had the money or access to look.

For a novice, a blank country is a question about who has counted, not a sign that children are safe. Ask whether any survey of children has been done there, and who would fund one.

ERI.story:
In 2025 the US clearinghouse for online child abuse reports, NCMEC, received 11 reports linked to Eritrea. Those reports come mostly from technology companies that find abuse material on their services. Eleven does not measure abuse in Eritrea; it reflects how few people there use the platforms that send reports, and how little reaches international systems from the country.

For comparison, in the same year the clearinghouse received 23.4 million reports in total, and 14% of them could not be placed in any country. North Korea had 12. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied data for 2023.

This map has no case of child abuse or trafficking recorded inside Eritrea. With so few reports and no survey, the record is close to empty.

For a novice, a very small number can be as uninformative as no number. Ask what a figure is counting before treating it as a measure of safety.
